President Donald Trump called the U.S. air traffic control system "ancient" during a press briefing following a major nationwide ground stop, and he fired White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross—following a wave of tech outages. #Trump #air #traffic #control #ancient  Sean Cairncross fired White House National Cyber Director FAA ground stop outage Kirsten Davies Trump $50 billion air traffic control Sean Duffy FAA outage Trump cyber chief fired US flight systems ancient Tech outages FAA banks NSA Why Trump Called Transportation Tech "Ancient" The Nationwide Ground Stop. On November 13, 2026, a telecommunications outage halted flights across the U.S. for four hours, delaying or canceling over 15,000 flights in the longest nationwide ground stop since 9/11.  Outdated Equipment. Speaking to reporters on November 20, Trump blamed the disruption on the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) infrastructure, calling it "ancient" and "obsolete" because much of the hardware and copper wiring is at least 55 years old. According to BBC News, Trump maintained the system is still safe because flights are spaced out and operated "very slowly," which he blamed for frequent airport delays. The Upgrade Glitches and $50 Billion Push. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy—who remains in charge of the Department of Transportation—explained that the outage began when a contractor swapping copper lines for fiber optics installed a router that malfunctioned and flooded the network. As reported by NewsNation, Trump told Duffy to stop spending money on temporary "patch" fixes and urged Congress to approve a $50 billion emergency overhaul to completely rebuild the air traffic control system.  Who Was Fired and Why The Official Removed. Neither Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy nor FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford was fired. Instead, on November 19, Trump removed Sean Cairncross, the White House National Cyber Director, replacing him with Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies. The Context of Widespread Outages. Cairncross's ouster followed a chaotic week of separate tech blackouts across both government agencies and major private corporations, including the FAA ground stop, a three-day outage on the National Security Agency's classified network, and major service disruptions at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, and Wells Fargo.  The Stated Reasons. When reporters asked Trump why he fired Cairncross, he replied bluntly, "Because I didn't think that person was good enough". According to CBS News, White House sources also noted that new Chief of Staff Stephen Miller had been pushing for Cairncross's removal because Cairncross—a former Republican National Committee official—lacked the technical cybersecurity credentials needed for the role.
